overview: This modern Iran record spans late Qajar rule, the Pahlavi monarchy and the Islamic Republic established in 1979. The atlas starts in 1920; neither Iran nor its societies began then. Its imported “Islamic Republic” alias is inappropriate for the earlier decades.

periods.title: Late Qajar years
periods.summary: The map opens before the 1921 coup and the replacement of the Qajar dynasty in 1925.

periods.title: Reza Shah’s monarchy
periods.summary: Centralized administration and expanding state institutions reshaped government, education and infrastructure.

periods.title: Mohammad Reza Shah
periods.summary: The second Pahlavi monarch ruled after his father’s forced abdication. Bureaucracy and royal authority expanded, with major political conflict.

periods.title: Revolution and war
periods.summary: The monarchy ended in 1979. An Islamic republic emerged, followed by the devastating war with Iraq.

periods.title: Constitutional revision and social change
periods.summary: The constitution was amended in July 1989. Its official-language provisions formed part of a framework within which diverse communities lived.

periods.title: Conflict and civilian needs
periods.summary: An August 2026 UNICEF report described disrupted health, water and sanitation services and emergency support for families.

items.text: Reza Shah’s administration kept official papers in offices instead of treating them as an official’s personal possessions. Written rules, specialized jobs and new departments made government more extensive. Yet the shah retained arbitrary personal authority: a larger filing cabinet did not necessarily mean more public control.
In 1951, support for nationalizing the oil industry helped bring Mosaddeq to the premiership. Oil revenues and foreign influence were major political issues.

The 1953 overthrow of Prime Minister Mohammad Mosaddeq had both Iranian participants and foreign organizers. CIA records released through the National Security Archive acknowledge the agency’s role in planning and carrying out the coup, with British involvement. The surviving files also show why historians debate the roles of particular actors.

Strikes, demonstrations and military defections undermined the monarchy in 1978 and 1979. After the shah left and Khomeini returned from exile, the monarchy collapsed. A referendum preceded the formal proclamation of the Islamic Republic on 1 April 1979.

The post-revolutionary system combined an elected president and parliament with a religious Leader and powerful supervisory bodies. The Library of Congress’s 2008 account describes the Guardian Council reviewing parliamentary legislation. Elections and clerical authority therefore operated together within a restricted political framework.

The Iran-Iraq War lasted from 1980 until a ceasefire took effect on 20 August 1988. UN observers monitored the ceasefire and withdrawal of forces toward internationally recognized boundaries. A line becoming quieter was an essential step toward recovery for communities that had endured years of war.

A UN mission’s September 2024 update linked nationwide “Woman, Life, Freedom” protests to the death in custody of Jina Mahsa Amini in September 2022. It reported intensified restrictions on women and girls and a lack of accountability. These were documented human-rights concerns, alongside women’s many contributions to social and intellectual life.

Built between 1927 and 1938, the Trans-Iranian Railway linked the Caspian region with the Persian Gulf across two mountain ranges. Iranian authorities worked with 43 contractors from several countries on the 1,394-kilometre route. Its scale made railway construction an international undertaking within a national state project.

The railway required 224 tunnels, including 11 spiral tunnels, as well as hundreds of bridges. A train could follow a winding route through difficult mountain country rather than a simple straight line. National taxes financed construction, part of a deliberate effort to avoid foreign financial control.

Secular schools expanded under Reza Shah, training people who could staff the growing administration. Learning also reached adults: the historical account records more than 150,000 people in evening programmes by 1940. School history includes grown-ups returning to lessons after their ordinary working day.

Maryam Mirzakhani received the Fields Medal in 2014 for breakthroughs in the geometry and dynamics of mathematical surfaces and the spaces used to study them. By then she worked at Stanford. Her achievement belongs to an Iranian life within international mathematics, rather than to a single country’s laboratory.

Mirzakhani had once wanted to become a writer. She won mathematics Olympiad gold for Iran in 1994 and returned with a perfect score in 1995. Later, she worked through problems by drawing on big sheets of paper; her daughter called it “painting.” Serious mathematics can involve a surprisingly large doodle.

Yalda/Chella, shared with Afghanistan, marks the last night of autumn. UNESCO’s 2022 description has families gathering at elders’ homes, with a lamp, water and red foods such as pomegranates and watermelon. Poetry, stories, music and games help fill the evening. The fruit bowl has a starring role.

For Nowruz, many families grow wheat or lentil shoots indoors before the spring celebration. The haft sin table brings together seven named items beginning with the Persian sound s, such as garlic, apples and vinegar. A UNESCO account describes fish and rice at the family meal, with the green sprouts at the table’s centre.

In the Fars weaving tradition documented by UNESCO in 2010, men sheared wool and made horizontal looms, while women spun yarn, chose colours and wove designs. Mothers taught daughters and fathers taught sons through demonstration. This describes a particular craft community’s division of work, not a rule for every Iranian household.

Fars carpet colours could come from plants including madder, indigo, walnut skins and pomegranate skins. The women described by UNESCO worked without a prepared design drawing, incorporating scenes from nomadic life. The finished floor covering was also a record of a maker’s choices, skill and surroundings.

On the northern Persian Gulf coast, hand-built wooden Lenj boats served fishing, trade, journeys and pearl diving. Navigators learned to use the sun, moon and stars, while named winds, wave heights and water colours helped them anticipate weather. Work songs were part of life aboard, too.

UNESCO’s 2011 account warned that cheaper fibreglass vessels and an ageing group of practitioners threatened Lenj knowledge. Some wooden-boat workshops were becoming repair shops. Saving a boat tradition meant passing on ways of building, reading weather and working together, as well as preserving the vessel itself.

sections.title: Health, schools and the small things that matter

items.text: A 2008 WHO report describes rural health houses staffed by trained local workers called behvarzan. They helped with vaccination, maternal and child health, sanitation and referrals to larger centres. Being from the community mattered: a worker could know both a family’s medical history and its everyday circumstances.

Health-house registers recorded household members, pregnancy histories, sanitation and children’s dental care. A circular chart tracked births, deaths and family-planning activity. This was practical information for preventive care; a small village office could help larger health services understand what families needed.

At Afjeh near Tehran, health worker Maryam Alaini told WHO in 2008 that her team served Iranian and Afghan-born villagers. Weekly school visits taught children about clean hair, nails, mouths and teeth. The same report recalls latrine-building work in 1975: health care also involved the surroundings in which people lived.

At Sanderos School in Birjand, a UNICEF story published in February 2025 described 340 Iranian and Afghan pupils learning water conservation through songs, stories and art. Children wore water-drop caps and carried the message home. Sometimes the person reminding a household to save water is its smallest member.

The Birjand story also describes repaired taps, drinking fountains and school restrooms. Third-grader Ahmad noticed the taps no longer leaked. Conservation lessons worked alongside repairs: telling children that water matters is more convincing when the school’s own plumbing cooperates.

In July 2023, UNICEF reported ten new classrooms across five schools in Khorasan Razavi and Sistan and Baluchistan, areas with many Afghan refugee pupils. Safe water points and separate latrines for girls and boys accompanied the classrooms. Room to learn and a usable toilet were parts of the same education project.

UNICEF’s 4 August 2026 report described conflict disrupting families’ access to health care, safe water and sanitation. Its response included mobile health units, vaccine refrigeration, water-purification supplies and counselling. This dated humanitarian account records civilian needs; it does not establish a final military or political outcome.

WIPO’s record of the constitution revised in 1989 gives its Persian title as قانون اساسی جمهوری اسلامی ایران. Transliteration: Qānun-e asāsi-ye Jomhuri-ye Eslāmi-ye Irān. Translation: “Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Iran.” This is a modern Persian document title, reproduced from an institutional catalogue, rather than an ancient inscription.

Article 15 calls Persian the country’s official and common language and script, while permitting regional and ethnic languages in media and the teaching of their literature alongside Persian. A language rule in a constitution is evidence about state policy, not proof that everyone at home spoke the same language.

ending.text: Iran’s history continues beyond the map’s last stored snapshot. Regime changes did not end its communities or cultures. Dated reporting here reaches August 2026 and describes serious civilian needs without predicting the country’s political future.
